newsitem.title: UK: New sell-off hits gold, oil and US wheat prices rally.
newsitem.headline: New sell-off hits gold, oil and US wheat prices rally.

text.p: A drop in the price of gold accelerated on Monday while oil and wheat rallied as commodity markets got back in stride after a Christmas and New Year lull.
Nickel also attracted investor interest.
Speculators had already marked the New Year with a vote of no confidence in gold when selling sent it to 3-/4 year lows last week, and Monday saw a fresh drop to a London close at $357.95 an ounce.
That was down some $10 from the last trading day of 1996. "This is the first week of the New Year and we're at three-year lows," said analyst Ted Arnold of Merrill Lynch.
"Increasingly it looks like the downside is wide open. In 1997 I think $330 looks possible."
Investment funds, anticipating lower prices, have sold gold heavily "short" and professional dealers followed the trend.
Expected buying by jewellery manufacturers, mainly from the Far East, also failed to support the market. Many buyers are standing aside and waiting for lower prices, dealers said.
Fear that some central banks may sell gold to meet economic criteria for European Monetary Union has also made investors wary of it.
Oil prices staged a new rally as forecasts of more cold weather created firm demand for heating oil in the United States.
London February futures for the bellwether Brent Blend of North Sea crude oil rose 53 cents to $24.65 a barrel, in sight of mid-October's post-Gulf War high, before easing slightly.
"The main feature is the renewed cold in the U.S. after a mild spell last week and continued cold temperatures in Europe," said a futures broker in London.
The weather in North America also led to a rally in wheat prices on the Chicago Board of Trade where the March contract put on 10 cents to $3.94 per bushel around midday.
"Unseasonably warm weather followed by very cold weather could produce some serious winterkill problems," said Victor Lespinasse, a vice-president with Dean Witter in Chicago.
Weekend warmth in the U.S. Southern Plains melted the dormant wheat crop's insulating snow cover. Crops are now more susceptible to freeze damage, traders said.
Three months delivery nickel on the London Metal Exchange (LME) posted gains on investment fund buying and shortcovering.
Prices at one stage reached $6,945 a tonne, the highest since December 3 and $340 above Friday's close as consecutive buy stops were triggered.
Traders and analysts said the bounce was largely due to a correction from a recent oversold condition.
Scrap material remains in short supply and an expected pick up in demand from the stainless steel industry, which accounts for 60 percent of nickel offtake, should underpin the market.
Most other commodities were less volatile.
